How it works

Pick a scenario from the list. Its panel shows how the AI was put to work step by step, who checked it, and which real tools you could use to build something similar.

Who acts at each step:PersonAIExpertOutcome
Scenarios
Case 01 · USA · Health

A general chatbot as a second opinion

A mother used an everyday chatbot to connect clues that 17 specialists, each looking at their own area, had not put together.

At a glance

The problem
Three years of unexplained pain in a young child, and no one doctor looking at the whole picture.
AI used
ChatGPT, a free general‑purpose chatbot. Nothing medical was added to it.
What goes in
MRI report notes typed in line by line, plus everyday observations, such as Alex refusing to sit cross‑legged.
What comes out
A suggested condition to investigate: tethered cord syndrome.
Who checks it
A neurosurgeon, who reviewed the existing MRI images.
Cost to the family
None beyond the free sign‑up.

Step by step

  1. Person

    Courtney gathers every record she has: MRI notes, symptoms, and behaviours no specialist had linked.

  2. AI

    The chatbot reads it all together and suggests tethered cord syndrome, a condition tied to a hidden form of spina bifida.

  3. Person

    She researches the condition and joins a Facebook group of families whose children have it. The patterns match.

  4. Expert

    A new neurosurgeon looks at the scans already taken and confirms it: occult spina bifida with a tethered spine.

  5. Outcome

    Alex has surgery to release the cord and begins recovering.

Why it worked

The AI looked across specialties at once, and the answer was already sitting in scans the family had.

Limits

Chatbots can be confidently wrong. This worked because the suggestion went to a specialist, not straight to treatment.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service. A prototype is for learning only: anything touching health needs clinical validation and regulatory approval.

Models
Claude, GPT‑4o or Gemini (hosted), or Llama and Mistral run locally with Ollama
Reading reports
PyMuPDF or Tesseract OCR to pull text out of scanned reports
Medical knowledge
Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) to map symptoms, and Orphanet for rare conditions
Interface
Streamlit or Gradio for a simple upload‑and‑ask web app
SourcesTODAY interview, via Radiology Business ↗Read the full case →
Case 02 · USA · Disability

Brain signals turned into his own voice

Sensors in Casey Harrell's brain pick up the commands his brain sends to his speech muscles, and AI turns them into spoken words.

At a glance

The problem
ALS left Casey understood only by his care partner, at about seven words a minute. Everyday talk runs near 160.
AI used
Neural networks trained on Casey's own brain activity, a language model, and text‑to‑speech built from old recordings of his voice.
What goes in
Electrical activity from four microelectrode arrays in the speech area of his brain.
What comes out
Words on a screen, read aloud in a voice that sounds like Casey before ALS.
Who checks it
The BrainGate clinical trial team at UC Davis Health.
Status
Research trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, 2024.

Step by step

  1. Expert

    July 2023: surgeons implant four microelectrode arrays in the left precentral gyrus, the area that coordinates speech.

  2. Person

    Casey tries to speak. The system reads the commands sent to his speech muscles, not his private thoughts.

  3. AI

    A neural network turns the signal patterns into phonemes, the small units of sound that make up words.

  4. AI

    A language model assembles the phonemes into the most likely words, drawing on a 125,000‑word vocabulary.

  5. AI

    Text‑to‑speech trained on recordings of his pre‑ALS voice reads each sentence aloud.

  6. Outcome

    About 97% of words decoded correctly. He was using it within minutes on the first day, and talks with family and friends again.

Why it worked

Decoding attempted muscle movements is more reliable than guessing thoughts, and a personal voice made the output feel like him.

Limits

It requires brain surgery and is still a research trial, not standard care.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service. A prototype is for learning only: anything touching health needs clinical validation and regulatory approval.

Practice data
Public intracortical speech datasets released by the BrainGate team (Brain‑to‑Text benchmarks)
Decoding
PyTorch recurrent networks that output phonemes, with CTC decoding
Language model
KenLM n‑gram models or a small open LLM to pick the likeliest sentence
Personal voice
Coqui XTTS or Piper to build a voice from old recordings
SourcesBrown University ↗Reuters, via The Daily Star ↗Read the full case →
Case 03 · Switzerland · Disability

A digital bridge across a spinal injury

Two implants and an AI decoder carry Gert‑Jan Oskam's intention to move past the break in his spinal cord.

At a glance

The problem
A cycling accident severed the link between his brain and the nerves that move his legs.
AI used
Adaptive decoding algorithms that learn, in real time, which movement he is trying to make.
What goes in
Brain signals recorded by WIMAGINE implants over the brain region that controls the legs.
What comes out
Stimulation commands sent wirelessly to an implant on the spinal cord below the injury.
Who checks it
Neurosurgeons and rehabilitation staff at CHUV and EPFL in Lausanne.
Status
Single‑participant study, published in Nature, 2023.

Step by step

  1. Expert

    Surgeons place WIMAGINE devices, developed by the French research agency CEA, above the leg area of the brain, and electrodes on the spinal cord.

  2. Person

    Gert‑Jan thinks about moving his hips, knees or ankles.

  3. AI

    Algorithms decode the intention from his brain signals and predict which muscles he wants to use.

  4. AI

    A portable unit sends the command wirelessly to the spinal implant, which stimulates the right muscles at the right moment.

  5. Expert

    He trains with the bridge in rehabilitation. Some nerve function returns, and he can move a little even with the system off.

  6. Outcome

    He stands, walks 100 metres or more, climbs stairs, and can stand at a bar with friends.

Why it worked

The system adapts to him quickly. He said he could control his hips within 5 to 10 minutes on the second day.

Limits

One participant, two surgeries, and the walking is still tiring. Wider trials are needed.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service. A prototype is for learning only: anything touching health needs clinical validation and regulatory approval.

Hardware stand‑in
A non‑invasive EEG headset such as OpenBCI or Muse
Signal tools
BrainFlow to stream data, MNE‑Python to clean and analyse it
Practice data
PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery dataset; the MOABB benchmark
Output
Drive a simulated leg in Unity, or a servo on an Arduino
SourcesCEA (French public research body) ↗ITV News ↗Read the full case →
Case 04 · England · Health

Faster stroke treatment from brain‑scan reading

AI reads stroke patients' brain scans the moment they're taken, so doctors anywhere can decide on treatment faster.

At a glance

The problem
A patient loses about two million brain cells a minute at the start of a stroke, and not every hospital has a specialist on site.
AI used
Brainomix e‑Stroke, decision‑support software endorsed by NICE in 2024.
What goes in
CT and CT angiography scans of the brain taken on arrival.
What comes out
A real‑time readout showing blocked large vessels, any bleeding, and how much of the brain is affected.
Who checks it
Stroke doctors make every treatment decision.
Scale
In use at all 107 stroke centres in England.

Step by step

  1. Person

    A patient like Shawn Theoff arrives with stroke symptoms and is scanned within minutes.

  2. AI

    The software analyses the scan in real time and flags a clot or a bleed, and how much brain tissue is at risk.

  3. Expert

    Stroke specialists see the results on their phones or computers, even from another hospital.

  4. Expert

    They decide on clot‑busting drugs, a clot‑removal procedure, or a transfer to a specialist centre.

  5. Outcome

    Treatment starts more than 60 minutes sooner, and the share of patients regaining independence rose from 16% to 48%.

Why it worked

It removes the wait for a specialist to see the scan in person, which matters most in the first hour.

Limits

NHS England calls these results an association from early analysis, not a controlled trial.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service. A prototype is for learning only: anything touching health needs clinical validation and regulatory approval.

Imaging AI
MONAI (PyTorch for medical imaging) and nnU‑Net for segmentation
Practice data
RSNA Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection and ISLES stroke lesion datasets
Remote viewing
Orthanc DICOM server with the OHIF web viewer
Desktop review
3D Slicer to inspect scans and model output
SourcesNHS England ↗Digital Health ↗Read the full case →
Case 05 · Sweden · Health

AI as the first reader of mammograms

AI scores every screening mammogram for risk, so radiologists spend their double‑checking where it matters most.

At a glance

The problem
Standard screening has two radiologists read every mammogram. That is slow, and some cancers still surface between screenings.
AI used
Transpara, a system trained on more than 200,000 exams from over ten countries.
What goes in
Routine screening mammograms.
What comes out
A cancer‑risk score from 1 to 10 for each exam, plus marks on suspicious areas.
Who checks it
Radiologists read every exam and decide every recall.
How we know
The MASAI randomised trial: over 105,000 women at four sites in south‑west Sweden.

Step by step

  1. Person

    A woman attends routine screening in Sweden's national programme.

  2. AI

    The AI gives her exam a risk score from 1 to 10 and marks any suspicious spots.

  3. Expert

    Exams scored 1 to 9 get one radiologist. Exams scored 10, the highest risk, get two.

  4. Expert

    Radiologists decide whether she needs further tests.

  5. Outcome

    29% more cancers found, mostly small and early. 12% fewer cancers found between screenings. Reading workload down 44%.

Why it worked

AI sorted the queue instead of making the call, so human attention went to the highest‑risk exams.

Limits

One country's programme. Results elsewhere depend on local screening practice.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service. A prototype is for learning only: anything touching health needs clinical validation and regulatory approval.

Practice data
CBIS‑DDSM, VinDr‑Mammo and the RSNA screening mammography dataset
Models
PyTorch with timm image models (EfficientNet, ConvNeXt), or MONAI
Marking areas
pytorch‑grad‑cam to show where the model is looking
Triage
A threshold rule in Python that sends the highest scores to double reading
SourcesPubMed record (Lancet Digital Health) ↗ecancer (full Lancet results) ↗Read the full case →
Case 06 · USA · Disability

Glasses that describe the world aloud

A camera in Chrichelle Brown's glasses lets an AI read and describe her surroundings when she asks.

At a glance

The problem
Everyday tasks like reading a sign or checking an outfit meant asking someone for help.
AI used
A multimodal AI assistant built into camera glasses, connected to the free Be My Eyes app.
What goes in
The live camera view and her spoken question.
What comes out
A spoken description, through speakers in the glasses' frame.
Who checks it
Chrichelle herself, using her training. A sighted volunteer is available through Be My Eyes.
Hands free?
Yes. She uses voice commands, not a phone screen.

Step by step

  1. Person

    She asks aloud, for example: “What's in front of me?”

  2. AI

    The camera captures the scene, and the AI identifies objects, reads text and describes the surroundings.

  3. AI

    The answer is spoken back through the glasses.

  4. Person

    If she's unsure, she can call a sighted volunteer through Be My Eyes.

  5. Outcome

    She can check how she looks and read signs on her own, and now teaches others at Columbia Lighthouse for the Blind.

Why it worked

A voice‑first, hands‑free design fits how blind people already move through the world.

Limits

The AI can misdescribe things. She teaches students to use it alongside their other skills, never instead of them.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service, mostly free or open source.

Seeing
Vision‑language models: GPT‑4o, Gemini or Claude, or LLaVA, Moondream and Qwen‑VL run locally with Ollama
Listening and speaking
Whisper for speech‑to‑text; Piper or eSpeak for text‑to‑speech
Reading text
Tesseract OCR as an offline fallback
Hardware
A phone, or a Raspberry Pi 5 with a camera module and earpiece
SourcesNBC Washington ↗Read the full case →
Case 07 · Nigeria · Learning

An after‑school AI tutor, guided by teachers

Secondary students in Benin City used a free chatbot as an English tutor, with teachers running every session.

At a glance

The problem
Large classes and limited one‑to‑one help. About 70% of 10‑year‑olds in low‑ and middle‑income countries can't read a simple text.
AI used
Microsoft Copilot, a free chatbot built on GPT‑4.
What goes in
Students' questions and writing, on topics teachers set from the English curriculum.
What comes out
Explanations, feedback on writing, and practice exercises.
Who checks it
Teachers guided every session and kept students on task.
How we know
A randomised evaluation by the World Bank across nine public schools.

Step by step

  1. Expert

    Teachers are trained to run the sessions and plan topics that match the term's English curriculum.

  2. Person

    Students attend twelve 90‑minute after‑school sessions over six weeks.

  3. AI

    Students ask the chatbot to explain grammar, give feedback on their writing and quiz them.

  4. Expert

    Teachers guide how students ask questions, check the AI's answers, and keep the work on the curriculum.

  5. Outcome

    Gains equal to 1.5 to 2 years of normal schooling, better end‑of‑term exams, and girls who started behind gained the most.

Why it worked

The AI added to the teaching rather than replacing it. Every extra session attended added to the gains.

Limits

A six‑week pilot in one city. Flooding and teacher strikes cut attendance for some students.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service, mostly free or open source.

Tutor
Open WebUI with Ollama on a school server, or any hosted chat model
Teaching style
A system prompt that asks questions back instead of giving answers
Curriculum
Retrieval over the syllabus with LlamaIndex and Chroma
Low connectivity
Kolibri (Learning Equality) for offline content
SourcesWorld Bank working paper ↗BusinessDay Nigeria ↗Read the full case →
Case 08 · USA · Work

A coach that whispers best practice

Support agents got live reply suggestions drawn from how the best agents handled similar problems.

At a glance

The problem
New agents take months to learn what experienced colleagues know about difficult cases.
AI used
A GPT‑based assistant trained on past support chats, learning most from the highest‑performing agents.
What goes in
The live customer conversation.
What comes out
Suggested replies and links to technical documentation, shown to the agent as the chat happens.
Who checks it
The agent decides whether to use, change or ignore each suggestion.
How we know
The tool was rolled out in stages, so economists could compare agents with and without it: 5,172 agents in all.

Step by step

  1. AI

    The assistant learns from a large set of past conversations, especially the top performers'.

  2. Person

    A customer writes in with a problem.

  3. AI

    The assistant reads the conversation in real time and suggests what to say next.

  4. Person

    The agent chooses whether to send it as written, edit it or ignore it.

  5. Outcome

    About 14–15% more issues resolved per hour on average, and 34% for the newest agents. Customers were politer, and staff stayed longer.

Why it worked

It passed experienced agents' know‑how on to newer agents, and the agent stayed in charge of every reply.

Limits

The most experienced agents gained little and saw small drops in quality.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service, mostly free or open source.

Retrieval
LlamaIndex or LangChain with Chroma, Qdrant or pgvector
Embeddings
sentence‑transformers models
Helpdesk
Chatwoot or Zammad, open‑source support desks you can add suggestions to
Practice data
Public customer‑support datasets on Kaggle and Hugging Face
SourcesNBER working paper ↗Read the full case →
Case 09 · Kenya & India · Work

An agronomist in a chat app

Smallholder farmers ask questions in their own language and get advice for their own plot.

At a glance

The problem
One extension officer per 1,000 farmers in Kenya and about 750 in India, so most farmers never get expert advice.
AI used
Chatbots on WhatsApp, phone lines and apps that combine a language model with checked farming guides and local data.
What goes in
A spoken or typed question in the farmer's language, or the farm's location.
What comes out
Specific advice: fertiliser amounts, intercropping plans, pest control and market prices.
Who checks it
The guides are vetted by agricultural experts, and in many programmes extension workers use the same tool.
Reach
FarmerChat alone has over 225,000 users in India, Ethiopia, Kenya and Nigeria.

Step by step

  1. Person

    A farmer like Sammy Selim sends his farm's coordinates, or asks a question by voice or text.

  2. AI

    Speech recognition and translation turn the question into text the model can work with.

  3. AI

    The model answers from vetted agricultural guides plus local weather, soil and market data.

  4. AI

    The reply is translated back and read aloud if needed. Sammy gets a target yield and the fertiliser mix to reach it.

  5. Person

    The farmer applies the advice. Extension workers use the same tool to reach more farmers.

  6. Outcome

    High satisfaction in a survey of over 800 farmers. Yield trials in Kenya run until January 2027.

Why it worked

It works on phones farmers already have, in their own language, including by voice for those who can't read.

Limits

Women farmers are less likely to own smartphones, and proof of higher yields is still being gathered.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service, mostly free or open source.

Phone line
WhatsApp Business Cloud API, or Twilio for voice calls
Languages
Whisper; AI4Bharat IndicConformer and IndicTrans2; India's Bhashini APIs
Answers
An LLM with retrieval over FAO and national extension guides
Local data
Open‑Meteo for weather, ISRIC SoilGrids for soil, Agmarknet for Indian market prices
SourcesThe Guardian, via NextBillion ↗ISDM case study ↗AIEP farmer study ↗J‑PAL trial ↗Read the full case →
Case 10 · USA · Paperwork

Help drafting an insurance appeal

Patients use AI to turn a denial letter and their records into a formal appeal they would otherwise never write.

At a glance

The problem
Appeals are technical and exhausting. Fewer than 1% of health‑coverage denials are ever appealed.
AI used
A free AI appeal assistant from the non‑profit Counterforce Health, and general chatbots.
What goes in
Usually the denial letter, the insurance plan's terms and the relevant medical records.
What comes out
A draft appeal letter that answers the insurer's stated reason.
Who checks it
The patient, ideally with their doctor, before it is sent.
Note
These steps describe how such tools generally work. Each tool differs.

Step by step

  1. Person

    A patient receives a denial and gathers the letter, the plan documents and their records.

  2. AI

    The AI picks out the reason for the denial and the parts of the plan that apply.

  3. AI

    It drafts an appeal that argues medical necessity and cites the records and plan terms.

  4. Expert

    The patient and their doctor check every medical fact before sending.

  5. Outcome

    Appeals get filed by people who would have given up. Some states have also barred insurers from letting AI alone deny care.

Why it worked

It takes the effort out of the process, which is what usually stops people appealing.

Limits

People without medical training may miss a factual error that sinks the appeal.

Build a similar prototype

Real tools you can use to build a learning prototype of this kind of service, mostly free or open source.

Reading letters
PyMuPDF and Tesseract OCR
Extraction
An LLM with structured (JSON) output to pull out the denial reason and plan terms
Drafting
python‑docx to fill an appeal letter template
Guidance
Appeal guides from state insurance departments and patient‑advocacy non‑profits
